analysis.one_liner: Requires rent-to-own stores to disclose total ownership costs and gives customers reinstatement and fee protections.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to set the first federal disclosure and fairness rules for rent-to-own stores, backed by 9 senators, died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let households take home furniture, appliances, and electronics with weekly or monthly payments and an option to eventually own the item, usually for far more than the cash price. This bill would have required merchants to state the total cost of ownership up front and on store tags, banned practices like wage assignments and repeated late fees on the same missed payment, and given customers a right to reinstate after missing a payment. It also would have blocked state laws that treat these deals as high-cost credit requiring an annual percentage rate disclosure.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households that use rent-to-own stores because they lack cash or credit — about 2.3 million U.S. households a year by the bill's own findings [S3]. They would have learned the true total cost before signing, kept the right to walk away without owing extra, and regained ownership rights after a missed payment [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Merchants must clearly disclose, before signing and on a tag at the point of rental, the cash price, each payment, the number of payments, and the total cost to acquire ownership [S3].

Agreements may not contain confessions of judgment, wage assignments, waivers of legal claims, or more than one late fee for the same missed payment, and merchants may not enter a home without consent to repossess [S3].
Customers who miss a payment get a defined window to reinstate the agreement and keep their progress toward ownership, and merchants cannot charge extra fees as a condition of taking ownership [S3].
The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, with civil liability and criminal penalties for willful violations [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own merchants bear the cost of new disclosure forms, store tags, advertising changes, and reinstatement rights [S3]. Consumers in states with stricter rules would also pay: the bill supersedes state laws that require an annual percentage rate disclosure or treat the transaction as credit [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill supersedes any state law requiring a percentage-rate disclosure such as an APR, and once the Federal Reserve deems a state provision inconsistent, merchants are exempt from it and face no liability under that state law [S3].

Companies that buy rental-purchase contracts can be sued only for violations visible on the face of the agreement, and a customer's signed acknowledgment of receiving disclosures is conclusive proof the disclosures were made [S3].
There is no cap on what a customer can be charged: the bill requires disclosure of the total cost but leaves rent-to-own prices free to run many multiples of the cash price [S3].

The bill's own findings describe the industry as meeting consumer demand and state a purpose of assuring the availability of rental-purchase transactions, framing that favors the merchants as much as their customers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure, reinstatement, and banned-practice provisions are real protections for a customer base with few alternatives, and honest supporters could defend them. But the bill is a bargain with the industry: it accepts federal rules in exchange for preempting state laws that treat rent-to-own as expensive credit, shields assignees from most lawsuits, and never touches the underlying cost of the product. A customer would learn the true price and still pay it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no further step.

narrative.text: Sen. Mary Landrieu introduced the bill on September 17, 2002, with eight cosponsors split between the parties [S5][S3].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which was the only action the bill ever received [S5].
No committee vote, hearing, or floor action followed before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own merchants came out ahead: no federal compliance costs were imposed, and nothing changed. Customers in states with weak protections kept getting agreements without clear total-cost disclosure, while the industry also failed to win the federal preemption it sought from stricter state rules.

for.name: Sen. Mary Landrieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: 5 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Breaux, Cleland, Lincoln, Conrad, Miller).

for.name: Rental-purchase industry
for.role: Rent-to-own chains and their trade associations (outside pressure)
for.what_they_did: The industry long sought federal legislation establishing uniform rental-purchase standards, which would shield it from state laws treating its contracts as high-cost credit; this bill's structure and findings track that agenda.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral the day it was introduced and never reported it, held no markup, and never voted.

against.name: Sen. Paul Sarbanes
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 3 Republicans, so the bill never got far enough for a party-line fight to appear; no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed real disclosure and fairness rules on stores serving low-income customers, but it also defines the transaction as a rental rather than credit and supersedes state laws requiring an annual-rate disclosure, locking in the industry's rental-not-credit business model nationwide. Its own findings praise the industry and pledge to assure its availability [S3].

Assignees could be sued only for violations apparent on the face of the agreement, and a customer's signed acknowledgment would be conclusive proof that disclosures were made, shielding the companies that buy these contracts from most customer lawsuits [S3].
